why: Shorter; cuts the self-narrated backstory and 'I used to think' framing, opens on the move and keeps the point.
B's 'fix is a guess that happens to compile' puts the student's work down; A states the positive mechanism (failing, then passing keeps the agent honest).
Cuts the trailing clause that restates the map; shorter, and a forward/orientation line about the course itself.
Cuts the forward pointer to Module 4 and the closer that announces the lesson; shorter, no course-about-itself line.
Shorter; the cut sentence narrates the agent's steps, a low-value restatement the author cuts freely.

B's added line is a trainer note that tells students to watch rather than type along, which makes them passive, and the line repeats the opening 'three plain questions'. A is shorter and keeps the student acting.
A is passive and patronizing ("Nobody can hand you", "gift you haven't given yet"); B keeps the student as the actor, which is the author's kept text.
B adds a low-value closer ("Three modules in, this is your practice now") that restates the point and congratulates the student; the shorter A wins.
Neither is the ideal 'spot-check', but 'Check what Claude proposes' fits the verifier theme and avoids implying the student reads every word.
The title states both the mechanism and the fix in plain words, while 'resets the chain' leans on a metaphor the title doesn't explain.
Plain 'ADR' line is concrete and shorter; B's 'future engineer can inspect' adds an abstract, wordier clause and pushes the term into parentheses.
Shorter header; 'context' is already clear from the body, so cutting a word reads faster.
Names the action in few words and cuts the lead-in that previews its own prompt, matching the author's AE101 cut.
A's 'which one you get depends on' makes the student passive; B's 'It will be what fits the session' is shorter and matches the author's past call.
Keeps 'alternative', the plain word; 'committed change' is a coined term, and B adds 'gives you the floor' and an extra example, so A is shorter.
The closing line 'One sentence buys the time back' is a kicker that adds little after the point, so the shorter version wins.
Cuts the low-value closing sentence; shorter wins and the author cuts restatements.
Less bolding and fewer emphasis markers keep it neutral; the content is otherwise identical and the quieter version reads faster.
